doc.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019

title: His daughter and the gig economy
summary: His filmmaker daughter works project to project, illustrating how the gig economy resembles musicians' lives.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: You have a 30-year-old daughter you said?
Did she learn the word “gig” early on, as a kid.
She learned the word “gig” right now because she’s in a gig economy.
The term has been usurped by economists and people who are writing. I mean now you see it in — she is a filmmaker.
I said, “What do you mean a gig economy?” And then it was explained to me and I said, oh yeah that’s what musicians —

That’s right. And she is a filmmaker and she is doing human rights work. She’s doing some really fascinating work, of course I’m very proud of her. But you know the assignments are a year, six months, four months, some of them have health insurance, some of them don’t, but they’re not a tenure track position for a company or a university. They’re until this project gets finished, and some projects are longer than others. And she is like in there doing it at a high level. But the whole parameter, the whole paradigm has shifted to a gig economy and now we’re going to start talking about economics and it’ll © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-
be a little bit of a diversion from the task here, but it’s really changing things a lot in this country and changing how we all look at our future.
